# Analysis

## Initial Thoughts

Chess is a complex game with a large branching factor, making it a fascinating challenge for programmers. The sheer number of possible moves and positions that can arise in a game of chess is immense, leading to an exponential growth in complexity as each move is made. This characteristic branching factor poses a significant computational challenge for designing efficient and intelligent chess-playing algorithms.

Chess engines are computer programs designed to play chess. They utilise sophisticated algorithms to analyse positions computing what it thinks to be the best move. Chess engines can play chess at a much higher skill level and much quicker than humans making them very useful in analysing games to help chess players improve quickly. Not only that but chess engines can be used as an opponent as their skill level can match any human’s skill level.

The aim of this project is both to investigate how to make a competent chess engine as well as to to help players improve both by providing them with opponents of any difficulty they can play against at any time and with analysis tools that allow players to go through their matches move by move to spot better moves that they could have made. Additionally, the chess engine can also be used to give players instant feedback of the move they make to help players improve their understanding of the game.

The chess engine can be interacted through a website with an appealing interface allowing it to be customised with different colours and chess pieces. The website will also act as a platform for users to upload games that they have played in real life to share with friends and to analyse. The website will use a database to store all games played so that user statistics can be calculated. Some statistics may include a player’s move accuracy (calculated by the chess engine).

## Pre-modelling

Chess engines use sophisticated algorithms and artificial intelligence techniques to calculate which move to make. Below are some of the key components of a chess engine that must be taken into consideration.

### Board representation

Chess engines should represent the chess board in a data structure that allows positions to be manipulated efficiently allowing fast move generation and position evaluation. One way of storing a chess board in memory is using a bitboards. A bitboard is a 64 bit unsigned integer representing an 8x8 board for a single piece.

To represent all the white and black pieces it will take 12 bitboards as there are 6 pieces for each colour. Additionally, more bitboards are used to represent all occupant squares, all white pieces, and all black pieces. Generating moves using bitboards can be done using bitwise operations to manipulate the bits. For example, to find some of the pawn moves for white the following C code can be applied to the WPawns bitboards:

| 0   | 0   | 0   | 0   | 0   | 0   | 0   | 0   |

Finding the attacks that the pawns could make can also be done easily by shifting the pawns left and then checking if there is a black piece there.

Another method for storing a board in memory is to use an array of length 64 with each element representing either the piece type or empty however this is usually less efficient as iteration must be used for move generation which dramatically slows down the search process.

### Search algorithms

A search algorithm is used to explore the decision tree of possible future moves from the current position. Search algorithms are required for a chess engine as finding the best move is very hard without being able to evaluate the positions that come from the current position. Search algorithms can be more selective than others with most modern chess engines being both

Below are some algorithms used to explore the game tree.

#### Depth-limited minimax

Minimax is a recursive depth-first search algorithm that looks ahead a certain number of moves giving a position a score where the one player tries maximising the evaluation and the other player minimising the evaluation. Figure 2 below shows a simplified example of a minimax of depth 2 ply.

![Minimax diagram.](data:image/jpeg;base64,)

Figure 2 Minimax diagram (Hartikka, 2017)

The pseudocode below shows negated minimax (negamax) a simplified version of minimax that can be applied to chess as max(a, b)= -min(-a, -b). The evaluation function must be modified to return the score relative to the side being evaluated.

int negaMax( int depth ) {

if ( depth == 0 ) return evaluate();

int max = -oo;

for ( all moves) {

score = -negaMax( depth - 1 );

if( score > max )

max = score;

}

return max;

}

(Isenberg, 2018)

#### Alpha-beta pruning

Pruning is an important process when searching through the decision tree as after just a few moves there are many different boards to be evaluated. After just three moves made by each player there are 119060324 moves, 809099 checks and 10828 checkmates.

Alpha-beta pruning reduces the number of positions that the bot will evaluate by cutting off a branch if it can no longer contain the best move. It has no effect on the outcome of minimax.

Figure 3 shows how alpha beta pruning can increase efficiency by evaluating less positions (when search is done in the order shown in the diagram).

![Minimax diagram with alpha beta pruning.](data:image/jpeg;base64,)

Figure 3 Minimax diagram with alpha beta pruning (Hartikka, 2017)

This is achieved by using two variables alpha and beta where alpha represents the best score found so far for the maximising player, while beta represents the best score found for the minimising player.

The pseudocode below shows how this would be implemented using negamax. When using negamax the alpha of minimising player becomes minus beta of the maximising player and the other way round.

int alphaBeta( int alpha, int beta, int depthleft ) {

if( depthleft == 0 ) return evaluate();

for ( all moves) {

score = -alphaBeta( -beta, -alpha, depthleft - 1 );

if( score >= beta )

return beta; // fail hard beta-cutoff

if( score > alpha )

alpha = score; // alpha acts like max in MiniMax

}

return alpha;

}

(Isenberg, 2021)

#### Quiescence search

One problem with just using a depth-limited minimax search is that the bot will stop analysing positions past the depth. This can lead to the horizon effect where the bot’s depth is too low to see that it is making a losing trade.

Quiescence search aims to reduce the chance of this happening by looking at all forcing moves past its given depth (captures and checks). This function is used after reaching a depthleft of 0 in minimax so that the engine searches the position past its given depth until it reaches a quiet position.

The following pseudocode shows a quiescence search function that continues to search positions if there are captures. This is called when the recursive minimax function reaches a depthleft of 0.

int Quiesce( int alpha, int beta ) {

int stand_pat = Evaluate();

if( stand_pat >= beta )

return beta;

if( alpha < stand_pat )

alpha = stand_pat;

until( every_capture_has_been_examined ) {

MakeCapture();

score = -Quiesce( -beta, -alpha );

TakeBackMove();

if( score >= beta )

return beta;

if( score > alpha )

alpha = score;

}

return alpha;

}

(Isenberg, 2021)

#### Monte Carlo Tree Search (MCTS)

MCTS is a search algorithm is another popular search algorithm used in various board games. It can be used as an alternative to the traditional minimax algorithm. MCTS is a probabilistic search algorithm that focuses on the most promising parts of the search space. This makes it effective in games with large branching factors.

MCTS consists of four strategic phases:

1. **Selection** - start at the root node (current position) and apply the UCT (Upper Confidence bound applied to Trees) formula to each child node to a given depth. UCT is used instead of pure randomness to deal with the flaw of the engine favouring a losing move with only one or few refutations.
2. **Expansion** – adds the child node with the highest UCT score if the child node has not already been visited. If it has been visited before then it performs selection again with the child node as the root node.
3. **Simulation** – random moves (playouts) are conducted from the newly expanded nodes until a terminal state is reached. Many of these simulations are performed, the results providing an estimate of the value of a position. Stronger chess engines may use a neural network to perform playouts.
4. **Backpropagation** – the results obtained from the simulations are then backpropagated up the tree.

These phases can be repeated for a predefined number of iterations or until a time limit is reached. As the algorithm explores more nodes and simulations, it converges towards a more accurate evaluation of move quality.

### Evaluation function

The evaluation heuristic scores how much better one colour is than the other assigning a numerical value to a position. One way of doing this is to just calculate how much material one colour is up. This evaluation function can then be improved by using a piece-squares table by giving each piece a bonus score based on the square it is on. However, this evaluation function is still very basic and modern chess engines consider a variety of factors. Below is a javascript implementation of stockfish’s evaluation (a powerful open-source chess engine) function. It has a smooth transition between the different scorings returned by each game phase evaluation (mg and eg). Theses scorings are then aggregated using weights corresponding to the middlegame and endgame.

function main_evaluation(pos) {

var mg = middle_game_evaluation(pos);

var eg = end_game_evaluation(pos);

var p = phase(pos), rule50 = rule50(pos);

eg = eg \* scale_factor(pos, eg) / 64;

var v = (((mg \* p + ((eg \* (128 - p)) << 0)) / 128) << 0);

if (arguments.length == 1) v = ((v / 16) << 0) \* 16;

v += tempo(pos);

v = (v \* (100 - rule50) / 100) << 0;

return v;

}

(hxim, 2020)

Later versions of stockfish use a NNUE (Efficiently Updatable Neural Network) to evaluate positions. The NNUE is a shallow neural network that takes advantage of there being minimal changes to the inputs of the network between evaluations.

Using a complex evaluation function on every node in the search tree can be very time expensive when searching to a great depth. Another solution to this problem (other than pruning) is reducing the time it takes to evaluate a position. A lazy evaluation function can be introduced by incrementally updating the evaluation of a position. If this basic scoring of the position is within the alpha and beta bounds it can be evaluated using a more advanced evaluation function. This means that moves which simply lose a piece are discarded quicker.

### Opening book and endgame tables

Chess engines may use a database of known opening moves and responses in both the early game and in end game.

- Opening book allows chess engines to play a variety of openings instead of making the same opening every match. This makes games more human-like and can reduce the time spent in the opening phase much like a human would.
- Endgame tables allows chess engines to make optimal moves in positions that are known to be forced wins, draws or losses. It also allows the chess engine to make moves much quicker.
- Currently there are endgame tables available for any position which has seven pieces or less totalling 423,836,835,667,331 unique legal positions in about 18 terabytes.

### Neural networks

Neural networks play a crucial role in modern chess engines. They have many different uses such as being used for the evaluation function and move selection in MCTS. Neural networks can be trained on large data sets of human-played games or can be trained by playing chess games itself and improving. For example, the chess engine AlphaZero was trained just by playing against itself many times and was able to beat all traditional chess engines. It only searches 80,000 positions per second and can beat chess engines such as stockfish that search 70 million per second showing how powerful a deep neural network can be.

### Parallelization

Parallel search is a method to increase search speed by using additional processors that traverse separate branches simultaneously. For instance, one way of dividing the task of alpha-beta search is to express each node as a thread until the maximum number of threads has been reached.

# Design

## UCI protocol

The following flowcharts show how the engine and GUI interact.  
UCI commands sent by the GUI to the engine are coloured purple.  
Engine responses are coloured yellow.

![A diagram of a computer program

Description automatically generated](data:image/png;base64,)![A diagram of a computer process

Description automatically generated](data:image/png;base64,)

The universal chess interface (UCI) is a protocol used for communication between a chess engine and a chess GUI. It is a standard supported by most engines and GUIs allowing different engines and GUIs to work seamlessly.

The UCI protocol specifies how the GUI sends commands to the engine and how the engine should respond.

**Brief overview**:

1. **Initialisation**: When the GUI starts it sends an ‘isready’ command and the ‘uci’ command to get make sure the engine is ready and then get the engine name and author.
2. **Setting position / make move**: The GUI sends the “position” command to tell the engine the current position. The current position can either be set by FEN notation and/or by listing the moves.
3. **Searching for moves**: The GUI sends the “go” command to instruct the engine to start searching for the best move. It can also include additional parameters such as time control, fixed depth, or maximum nodes to search.
4. **Engine output**: As the engine searches it sends its current search state back to the GUI including information such as the current depth, principal variation and nodes searched.
5. **Best move**: After either the GUI tells the engine to stop, or a constraint has been reached the engine will return the best move.

## Algorithms

### Minimax vs MCTS

- **Depth of search**: Minimax with alpha-beta pruning can potentially search deeper into the game tree compared to MCTS. This depth can lead to better evaluations of positions.
- **Deterministic behaviour**: Minimax provides deterministic behaviour, meaning that given the same initial position and time constraints it should compute the same move.

### Move ordering

#### **MVV LVA** (**M**ost **V**aluable **V**ictim – **L**east **V**aluable **A**ggressor)

Simple heuristic to sort captures in an order that will make it more likely to find beta cut-offs earlier so that the engine is able to find the best move evaluating fewer nodes. This is done by considering captures where the source piece has a low score, and the target piece has a high score. For example, the move pawn capturing queen would be considered before pawn capturing bishop.

#### Killer move heuristic

Quiet moves that cause a beta-cutoff are stored as killer moves. When searching in a branch the same ply distance from the root the killer move is considered first. This assumes that most of the moves do not change the situation on the board too much. Killer moves are usually implemented as a 2D array with 2 slots for killer moves for every ply.

### Null move pruning

Search space can be reduced by making a null move and seeing if the resulting position is still strong. If this is the case, then it is not worth exploring further saving time. R, the depth reduction value is crucial in determining how deep the null move search goes, balancing between efficiency and accuracy. However, this fails in zugzwang situations (positions where it is disadvantageous to make a move).

### Iterative deepening

A time management strategy that searches all the depths up to the given depth rather than searching at the given depth immediately. This allows the engine to return the best moves after a given amount of time rather than waiting for the engine to complete a search at a fixed depth. Additionally, iterative deepening can be faster as results from previous searches are saved in the principal variation table and are explored first reducing the number of nodes searched.

The principal variation is the sequence of moves that the computer considers to be the best for both players.

### Principle variation search

An enhancement to the alpha-beta algorithm improving the efficiency of the search process by making educated assumptions about the best moves to explore.

In alpha-beta search, nodes in the game tree are classified on the values of two parameters (alpha and beta). These parameters define a window within the search aims to find the best possible move. If a move falls outside the window it is, consider either too good (fail high) or too bad (fail low) to be of interest.

PVS operates on the premise that if a promising move (PV move) is found early in the search, subsequent moves are likely to be less desirable. This assumption is based on the expectation that good move ordering will prioritise the most promising moves early in the search.

When a PV move is identified, PVS conducts a more focused search around this move, using a narrower window compared to the standard alpha-beta search. This narrower window aims to quickly prove that the other moves are inferior to the PV move, leading to faster cutoffs and a more efficient search.

However, if a move returns a score outside this narrowed window, indicating that the assumption was incorrect, PVS reverts to a standard alpha-beta search to explore the alternative moves more thoroughly.

### Transposition tables

A transposition table is a database that stores the score of recently evaluated positions. If the engine encounters a position in the transposition table, it can retrieve the stored evaluation from the transposition table rather than re-evaluating the position saving computational time.

**Zobrist hashing** is used to return an almost unique index for any chess position with the requirement that two similar positions generate entirely different indices.

**At Initialisation:** An array of 781 (12x64 + 1 + 4 + 8) pseudorandom numbers is generated

- One number for each piece-square combination
- One number for side to move
- Four numbers for castling rights
- Eight numbers to indicate file of en passant

**At Runtime**: To get the Zobrist hash for a position all numbers linked to the position are XORed together. For example, to get the hash for the start position:

\[white Rook a1\] xor \[white knight b1\] xor \[white bishop c1\] xor … (all pieces)

… \[white king castling\] xor \[white queen castling\] xor … (all castling rights)

Incremental updates can be done to the hash key as xor operations can be undone. For example, if white made the move e2e4 from the start position getting the new hash can be done as follows:

\[original hash\] xor \[white pawn e2\] xor \[white pawn e4\] xor \[side to move\]

### Move generation

Generating legal moves is a fundamental part of any chess engine. Moves can be generated efficiently with a bitboard board representation by first generating pseudo-legal moves. To go from pseudo-legal moves to full legality the move is pushed and if the king (of the side who just moved) is in check then it is not a legal move.

#### Leaping pieces

Generating pseudo-legal moves for leaper pieces (pawn, knight, king) is easy. Moves for these pieces can be generated by simply applying logical shifts to the bitboard of that piece to get a mask. Checks are also done to ensure that the move does not go outside the bounds of the board.  
Here is a function to return a mask for knight moves:

U64 mask_knight_attacks(int square) {

U64 bitboard = 0ULL | (1ULL << square);

return 0ULL | ((bitboard >> 17) & not_h_file)

| ((bitboard >> 15) & not_a_file)

| ((bitboard >> 10) & not_hg_file)

| ((bitboard >> 6) & not_ab_file)

| ((bitboard << 17) & not_a_file)

| ((bitboard << 15) & not_h_file)

| ((bitboard << 10) & not_ab_file)

| ((bitboard << 6) & not_hg_file);

}

To make the move generation process more efficient arrays are used storing the attack mask of each leaper piece on each square so that getting the mask is just one look up. These arrays can quickly be generated during initialisation of the chess engine.

U64 pawn_attacks\[2\]\[64\];

U64 knight_attacks\[64\];

U64 king_attacks\[64\];

void init_leapers_attacks() {

for (int square = 0; square < 64; square++) {

pawn_attacks\[white\]\[square\] = mask_pawn_attacks(white, square);

pawn_attacks\[black\]\[square\] = mask_pawn_attacks(black, square);

knight_attacks\[square\] = mask_knight_attacks(square);

king_attacks\[square\] = mask_king_attacks(square);

}

}

To get the moves from a mask the least significant bit can be popped until it is empty.  
Here is an example of generating knight quiet moves:

void knight_quiet_moves(struct Moves\* move_list, U64 bitboard, U64 empty) {

U64 nTargets;

while (bitboard) {

int fromSquare = lsb_index(bitboard);

bitboard &= bitboard - 1; // Remove lsb

nTargets = knight_attacks\[fromSquare\] & empty;

while (nTargets) {

int toSquare = lsb_index(nTargets);

nTargets &= nTargets - 1; // Remove lsb

// Add encoded move to move list

add_move(move_list, encode_move(fromSquare, toSquare, …));

}

}

}

#### Sliding pieces

Generating moves for sliding pieces is more complex than leaping pieces as we must consider other pieces that may block the piece’s attack. Magic bitboards, a perfect hashing algorithm, solves this issue.

Here are the steps to generate the moves using magic bitboards from the Chess Programming Wiki:

- Mask the relevant occupancy bits to form a key. For example, if you had a rook on a1, the relevant occupancy bits will be from a2-a7 and b1-g1.
- Multiply the key by a "magic number" to obtain an index mapping. This magic number can be generated by brute-force trial and error quite easily although it isn't 100% certain that the magic number is the best possible (see step 3).
- Right shift the index mapping by 64-n bits to create an index, where n is the number of bits in the index. A better magic number will have less bits required in the index.
- Use the index to reference a preinitialized move database.

- **Short**: Minimize code duplication. Multiple features from each parameter declaration. Fewer bugs.

#### Security

##### Hashing

Hashing passwords is a crucial security measure in protecting passwords. The process involves applying a mathematical function to the password string to output a hash value. This is a one-way process as it is not computationally feasible to reverse the process.

Hashing is applied to passwords before inserting into the database so that if hackers gain access to the database, they only have the hashes not the passwords themselves.

To confirm that the user has inputted the correct password their input is hashed and compared to the password hash in the database.

Passwords will be hashed using the bcrypt hashing algorithm. This is done for the following reasons:

- **High security**: bcrypt is designed to be a slow hashing algorithm, making it computationally expensive for attackers to brute force passwords.
- **Ease of implementation**: bcrypt can be quickly implemented in python using the library
- **Community endorsement**: bcrypt has been extensively reviewed and endorsed by security experts and is widely regarded as a secure choice for password hashing.

##### JSON web tokens

JWT is an open standard defining a compact and self-contained way to securely transmit information between parties as a JSON object. The information is digitally signed and so can be verified by the server using the secret key.

I will be using JWT for authorising users by giving them a JWT upon logging in. Once the user has logged in, each request will then contain the JWT in the headers. This means the server knows whether to give the user access to API endpoints. The JWT payload will contain the time the token was issued at, the expiration date and the user id. When the JWT expires, the user will need to receive a new one by logging in again.

##### Rate limiting

Rate limiting is a technique used to control the rate at which the client can make requests to the server. This is useful for preventing malicious users from abusing the API creating scripts to overwhelm it with excessive requests which could cause it to slow down or crash.

This can be done by using a sliding window rate limiter that tracks requests made by either a user or an ip address over a fixed time period. For example, the limit for the create user endpoint may be set to 3 requests for every minute.

## Database Overview

### PostgreSQL

I will be using PostgreSQL, a powerful open-source relational database management system (RDBMS), to store data for the chess website.

Advantages:

- **Scalability**: PostgreSQL can handle large amounts of data and concurrent users, making it suitable for the website if many users are accessing resources simultaneously
- **ACID Compliance**: PostgreSQL ensures data integrity with its support for ACID (Atomicity, Consistency, Isolation, Durability) transactions
- **Support for complex queries**: PostgreSQL supports complex queries including advanced SQL operations such as joins, subqueries and window functions. This is valuable for generating statistics, leaderboards, and other analytics for the website

## Programming style

- Procedural programming
  - **Modularisation**: Breaks down the program into smaller sections
  - **Abstraction**: Procedures abstract away implementation details once coded
  - **Debugging**: typically easier to debug as each procedure can be test individually and logical flow of the program is more explicit and easier to follow
- Defensive programming
  - **Error checking**: thorough validation and checking of inputs, outputs, and intermediary states to ensure they conform to expected conditions and constraints.
  - **Handling invalid inputs**
  - **Exception handling**
  - **Fail-safe defaults**
  - **Logging**
  - **Documentation**
- Modularised code
  - **Separate files** for procedures with **distinct functionalities** and components
  - Each module **encapsulates** this functionality
  - Modules have a clear interface **abstracting** away the details once it is created
  - **Debugging** is made easier as individual modules can be tested rather than the program as a whole
  - Modules can be **reused** so that code is not repeated
  - Each module can be **documented** making it easier to understand utilise them
- Whitespace
  - C compiler ignores whitespace however it is important to use it carefully as it can make the code more readable.
  - **Tabs** should be used visually represent the structure of the code indicating blocks of code such as function, loops, and conditions
- Comments
  - **Clarity and conciseness**
  - **Avoid redundancy**
  - **TODO and FIXME comments**
  - **Consistent style and formatting**
- Snake case
  - **No spaces or punctuation**
  - **Consistency**

## Data structures

### Board structure

Here is a possible C struct that can be used to store the state of a position.

struct Board {

&nbsp;   U64 bitboards\[12\];

&nbsp;   U64 occupancies\[3\];

&nbsp;   int side;

&nbsp;   int enpassant;

&nbsp;   int castle;

};

- 12 bitboards are required for each coloured piece
- One bitboard for all white pieces, one for all black pieces and one for both white and black
- The turn to move is either 1 or 0
- An integer is required to store the index of the square for enpassant if there is one available. This is done by setting the enpassant variable to the square behind the pawn that has been pushed two squares.
- Castling rights requires a 4-bit integer, two bits for each side of which are one for king side and one for queen side. Bitwise operations can be get and set a castling right.
